newsitem.title: CHINA: HK securities regulator criticises merchant banks.
newsitem.headline: HK securities regulator criticises merchant banks.

text.p: Hong Kong's Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) said on Friday it may take disciplinary action against some merchant bankers who were not doing their jobs well in advising clients and were misleading the regulator.

"Yes, there are merchant bankers or corporate financers who are misleading the regulator, either deliberately or because they haven't done enough work and it has to stop," SFC executive director Mark Dickens told reporters.
"Financial advisers' job is to ...tell the client what it has to do and then get the regulators into dialogue," Dickens, in charge of the enforcement division of the securities regulator, said.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index had a record breaking rally this week with the index rising 721.10 points, or 4.61 percent, on the week to post a closing high of 16,379.22 on Friday.
"We have had months where stocks have been doubling, tripling and in some cases, quadrupling," Dickens said.
But he said market activity was more worrying, with turnover reaching record highs.
Dickens said the corporate finance industry had come under considerable client pressure to get deals done, with the Hong Kong market active, leaving them less time to do due diligence checks.
"The more time they spend investigating one company making sure they are comfortable with the deal and with the numbers, the more deals they are missing out on," he said.
By not maintaining their usual level of scrutiny, merchant bankers were deferring disciplinary action and inquiry actions to the front line market regulator, he said.
"The self-regulation system comes under a great degree of stress," said Dickens.
The problem had been serious enough that the commission's corporate finance section wasted a lot of time trying to find out the facts and being misled, he said.

Recent high trading volume on the Hong Kong stock exchange, where turnover rose to a record on Thursday, and the changing nature of the market from one dominated by institutional investors to a concept-driven market dominated by retail investors had increased the complexity and difficulties of the regulator's job, Dickens said.
"It takes us longer and longer to screen through the prices and there are more and more people coming into the market that haven't been there before with no track record," he said.
Dickens said market regulators were worried that these new, big traders would engage in misconduct and they were concerned about their very speculative and aggressive investment strategy.

Average daily traded volume on the Hong Kong stock exchange reached HK$14.97 billion in the second quarter, up 2.95 times from HK$3.79 billion in the same period last year. Brokers say individual investors have boosted daily turnover in the market.

SFC chairman Anthony Neoh said last week that the Hong Kong market was in danger of being regarded as the 'Wild West of the East' by the international financial press, because a small number of players were intent on breaking the rules.
"In any market there will be speculative trading in a few stocks or in certain sectors at different times," Stock Exchange of Hong Kong chief executive Alec Tsui said this week.
Dickens said the SFC and Stock Exchange of Hong Kong were doing everything they could, such as suspending trading of stocks and issuing new regulations, to deter misconduct.
There were 21 stocks suspended last week either due to unusual share price and turnover fluctuations or pending corporate statements.

"The whole way the system is designed in Hong Kong, it is just not our job, it is everyone's job. That's what self-regulation means. We are the regulator, particularly my area, of last resort," Dickens said. Hong Kong Newsroom (852) 2843 6369
